clue.text: Producing a lot of fear? Very much

blocks.note: read literally: full of the thing that frightens
an everyday intensifier, as in '___ sorry'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether something is terrifying and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the first half is a pun: split the word and it is literally 'fully dread-inducing'. The second half is the ordinary intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Dreadfully' is a common intensifier meaning very much, as in 'dreadfully late'.

clue.text: Appreciates accommodation

blocks.note: slang for likes, as in 'she really ___ jazz'
British informal for lodgings, a rented room

explanation.surface: Someone is grateful for being given a place to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated slang senses; 'digs' for lodgings is everyday British, especially for students and touring actors.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig something is to like it, and digs are rented rooms.

clue.text: Gross dollop of Béarnaise

indicators.note: a dollop is a portion scooped out, so a piece of the next word is taken

blocks.note: the four letters after the B, inside the sauce's name

explanation.surface: Someone recoils at a disgusting blob of sauce on their plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' looks like 'disgusting' but is the verb: to gross is to earn before deductions.
explanation.definitionFit: A film that grosses a million earns a million before costs are taken off.

clue.text: Part of salad board in actor's space

blocks.note: to board and to room both mean to lodge somewhere as a paying guest

explanation.surface: Some salad and a board are set out in a performer's backstage room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' looks like a plank or a food board beside the salad; it is the verb meaning to lodge, which is also what 'room' means as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressing room is the backstage room where an actor gets changed and made up.

clue.text: Get mad? Aunt rethinks anger at heart

definitions.note: 'Get mad' here means make someone mad, a transitive verb like UNHINGE

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle, applied to each of the three words

explanation.surface: An aunt cools down and reconsiders her anger rather than losing her temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At heart' covers all three words before it, not just 'anger'. 'Get mad' reads as become angry, but the answer is the causative: to get someone mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative: a door off its hinges no longer works, so a mind knocked off its hinges has gone mad.

clue.text: Monarchy taking part in raffle: so thoughtful!

indicators.note: the answer is part of the words that follow

blocks.note: runs from the end of 'raffle' through 'so' into the start of 'thoughtful'

explanation.surface: Praise for a royal family that joins in a charity raffle.
explanation.walkthrough: Lesotho is a kingdom in southern Africa, entirely surrounded by South Africa, so 'Monarchy' is a fair definition for the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesotho is a kingdom with a reigning king, so it is a monarchy.

clue.text: Milky duck, mate?

definitions.note: 'Milky' is an adjective; OPAL is used attributively for the milky colour, as in 'opal glass'

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A cheery greeting to a duck, as if calling it 'mate'.
explanation.walkthrough: Opal glass is the milky white translucent kind, named for the gem's cloudy sheen.
explanation.definitionFit: Opal describes a milky, cloudy white, like the gemstone.

clue.text: Academic reimagined islets – to no avail

definitions.note: 'to no avail' is an adverbial phrase; PROFITLESS is the adjective 'of no avail'

indicators.note: to reimagine is to form again differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A scholar's reinterpretation of some small islands turns out to be a waste of effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Academic' looks like an adjective describing the reimagining; it is the noun, a university teacher, shortened to PROF.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done to no avail brings no benefit: it is profitless.

clue.text: Raw, one careens with luge and sweats, perhaps

indicators.note: to careen is to lurch wildly, so the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: A bobsledder's nightmare: someone skin-raw hurtles out of control on a luge and breaks into a sweat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweats' looks like perspiring after the luge run; it is the noun, sweatpants and sweatshirts. 'Perhaps' marks them as one example of lounge wear.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweats (tracksuit-style sweatpants and tops) are a kind of loungewear, clothes for relaxing at home.

clue.text: Around forest, finally decomposing, socks that'll feed plants

indicators.note: the last letter of 'decomposing'
used loosely: the G is set about, next to, the forest

blocks.note: the Forest of Arden, in Warwickshire and in Shakespeare's As You Like It

explanation.surface: Rotting socks buried around a wood are meant to act as fertiliser.
explanation.walkthrough: ARDEN is the crossword's stock forest. 'Feed plants' suggests compost, which is why decomposing socks seem to fit, but it means water them.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden hose is what waters, or feeds, the plants.

clue.text: Time flying saucer returned to give us something to eat

indicators.note: sent back, so the letters run the other way

explanation.surface: A flying saucer comes back to Earth bearing food for the humans.
explanation.walkthrough: A flying saucer is the everyday picture of a UFO, which is the abbreviation the clue wants turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tofu is bean curd, a food.

clue.text: Terrible scene, woven on goddam weaving device

indicators.note: threads are interlaced when woven, so the letters are mixed

explanation.surface: Someone curses a terrible tapestry being made on a blasted loom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woven' and 'weaving' sit side by side, but only the first is an instruction; the second belongs to the definition of LOOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Doom and gloom is a thoroughly bleak, depressing situation.

clue.text: Incognisant – unsettled – backing

indicators.note: disturbed, so the letters are moved

explanation.surface: Someone unaware of what is going on feels unsettled and backs off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like retreating; it means supporting.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanctioning a plan is backing it, giving it official approval.

clue.text: Cricketers botched friendlies

indicators.note: done badly, so the letters are messed up

explanation.surface: A cricket team makes a mess of its warm-up matches.
explanation.walkthrough: Infielders are the fielders placed close to the batsman; a friendly is a match that counts for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Infielders are cricketers fielding near the wicket.

clue.text: Aloof crossword setter's public image, ultimately: awful

indicators.note: at the end, so the last letter

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself: I'm
the face one shows the world

explanation.surface: A sour review: the setter's standoffish public persona is dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossword setter's' is the setter's I plus the 'S of 'is', giving I'M; it looks like a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone impersonal is cold and detached, aloof.

clue.text: Long time back, Everyman's included as potential success

indicators.note: going back in time suggests going backwards, so the word for a long time is written from its end
something included is taken in, so this piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the setter Everyman saying what belongs to him: mine

explanation.surface: An old story about a crossword setter's past entry that nearly won something.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the name this crossword's setter signs with, so 'Everyman's' means the setter's own possession, as the setter would say it.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose definition by role: someone shortlisted for an award has a chance of winning it but has not yet.

clue.text: I'm surprised seeing Frenchman with salad, as a rule

explanation.surface: Someone is taken aback to see a Frenchman eating coleslaw, which he usually does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' reads as 'usually', but 'a rule' is the definition: Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ohm's law is a rule of physics: voltage equals current times resistance.

clue.text: How you may draw back, wanting time: mistakenly

indicators.note: lacking, so the T is taken out

explanation.surface: An artist is told they may pull back a line they drew wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw back' looks like drawing but means recoil, and you recoil IN TERROR; with the T gone, IN ERROR is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Done in error means done by mistake.

clue.text: Hoofed mammals travelled to this place in East London

indicators.note: a Cockney accent, which drops the H of 'here'

blocks.clueFragment: travelled to this place in East London
blocks.note: rowed = travelled by boat; 'ere = here, as a Cockney says it

explanation.surface: A group of deer have journeyed to East London.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the traditional working-class accent of East London, and it drops initial H. 'Travelled' has to be the narrower 'rowed' to match the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Roe deer are a small species of deer, hoofed mammals; the name serves as a plural.

clue.text: Is the writer tucking into fish somewhere on the Med?

indicators.note: to tuck something into a thing is to push it inside, so these words go within the fish

blocks.note: the fish, split around the insert
the writer of the clue: I

explanation.surface: A question about whether the writer is eating fish at a Mediterranean resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' looks like eating the fish; it means going inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a North African country on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Language used when specifying a kind of bath

definitions.text: used when specifying a kind of bath

blocks.clueFragment: used when specifying a kind of bath
blocks.note: the national adjective that names the steam bath with massage

explanation.surface: A remark on the word people use to name a type of bath.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is an adjective hiding in a phrase: the word you put before 'bath' is also a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Turkish is the language of Turkey, and a Turkish bath is a steam bath followed by a wash and massage.

clue.text: Blow a fuse, as you did with News of the World, Mr. Murdoch?

definitions.text: as you did with News of the World, Mr. Murdoch?

blocks.clueFragment: as you did with News of the World, Mr. Murdoch?
blocks.note: a rag is a newspaper, and Rupert Murdoch lost his News of the World

explanation.surface: Someone asks Rupert Murdoch whether he flew into a rage over his newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The News of the World was a British Sunday tabloid owned by Rupert Murdoch, closed in 2011 after the phone-hacking scandal; 'rag' is slang for a newspaper, so he literally lost his rag.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose one's rag is British slang for losing one's temper, blowing a fuse.

clue.text: Nail that may be put to use in stable

definitions.text: that may be put to use in stable

blocks.note: a short nail with a large head

blocks.clueFragment: that may be put to use in stable
blocks.note: a stallion kept for breeding is 'put to ___'

explanation.surface: A nail that might come in handy around the stable.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a carpenter fixing the stable; the second sense is the stallion put to stud.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is both a large-headed nail and a stallion used for breeding.

clue.text: Most of cheek in undergarments

indicators.note: most of a word is nearly all of it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: cheek means nerve, the same word as the yellow metal; drop its last letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky display of underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass here is British informal for cheek or nerve, as in 'the brass neck of it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: the brassiere, shortened, is one kind of underwear.

clue.text: Seabird or two, as we can hear

indicators.note: spoken, the answer matches the sound of another word

blocks.note: 'two' means the answer to 2 Down, EARN

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they hear one or two seabirds calling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or two' looks like 'one or two'; it is a cross-reference to 2 Down, whose answer EARN sounds just like ERNE.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the white-tailed sea eagle.

clue.text: Hot Priest, we're told, achieved a noisy mode of transport

indicators.note: heard, not read, so the spelling follows the sound

blocks.note: Eli, the priest in the Book of Samuel
to cop is British slang for to get or obtain

explanation.surface: Gossip that the 'Hot Priest' (the TV character from Fleabag) managed to get a noisy ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot Priest' is the fan name for Andrew Scott's priest in Fleabag, so the pair reads as one person; it splits into H and ELI.
explanation.definitionFit: A helicopter is a famously loud aircraft, a mode of transport.

clue.text: Soft, incredibly lustrous kimono at the outset?

definitions.text: Soft, incredibly lustrous kimono at the outset?

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so each word gives only its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A description of a beautifully soft, shiny kimono.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the first letters spell SILK, and the clue describes what silk is, the classic kimono fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: As an &lit the whole clue reads straight: softness and sheen are the fabric's hallmarks, and it is the traditional kimono cloth.

clue.text: Who shouted 'Eureka!' and screamed 'Hi!' running around?

indicators.note: moving about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The story of the man who leapt from his bath shouting 'Eureka!' and ran through the streets yelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the legend itself: Archimedes supposedly ran naked through Syracuse after his bath-time discovery.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' on discovering displacement in his bath.
